identity.title: Position: The AI Conference Peer Review Crisis Demands Author Feedback and Reviewer Rewards

problem.claim: Major AI conferences face submission volumes above 10,000 papers per venue alongside concerns about review quality and reviewer responsibility.

gap.claim: The traditional one-way review system lacks a proposed accountability loop in which authors assess reviews and reviewers receive formal accreditation or rewards.

contributions.claim: Argues for transforming peer review into a bi-directional feedback loop that shares responsibility across authors, reviewers, and the conference system.
Proposes a two-stage bi-directional review process allowing author evaluation of reviews while minimizing retaliation, plus systematic rewards intended to incentivize review quality.

stated_novelty.claim: The paper distinguishes its reform proposal through the combination of author review-quality evaluation, anti-retaliation staging, and systematic reviewer rewards.

narrative_sequence.summary: Identifies unprecedented submission growth and concerns about review quality and responsibility.
Argues that peer review should become a bi-directional accountability loop involving authors, reviewers, and the conference system.
Focuses on reviewer accountability through staged author feedback and systematic rewards, while assigning other issues to policy enforcement, detection tools, or self-reflection.
Requests strong community interest in the problems and proposed reforms.

source_observation.claim: The proposal pairs author evaluation of reviews with safeguards against retaliation and reviewer incentives.

lessons.interpretation: Accountability mechanisms may need procedural protections and positive incentives to address predictable participation risks.
lessons.application: When proposing governance reform, specify both the feedback channel and safeguards or incentives governing its use.
lessons.exception: This framing may be unsuitable when feedback participants cannot be reliably protected or incentive effects cannot be monitored.

unknowns: The abstract reports no empirical evaluation, proof, deployment results, or comparison with alternative reforms.
The operational design and effectiveness of the two-stage process, accreditation, and rewards are unspecified.
The abstract does not establish that the proposal is novel relative to prior peer-review reforms.
